scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants the value of collaboration while arguing group work should not largely replace lectures; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Many classrooms still rely mostly on a teacher speaking while students listen.
One claim holds that group assignments should replace a substantial amount of lecture-based teaching, on the reason that students must gain experience collaborating with peers.
I agree that collaboration is valuable, but I do not believe group work should replace a substantial part of lectures.
First, the reason behind the claim is sound, since collaboration is a vital skill.
Working in groups teaches students to share ideas, divide tasks, and solve problems together.
For example, a group project can teach teamwork that a silent lecture never could.
This shows that collaboration prepares students for work, where people rarely succeed alone.
Group work also lets students learn from one another, not only from the teacher.
Explaining an idea to a classmate can deepen a student's own understanding.
To this extent, group assignments deserve a real place in education.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why lectures are still needed

sentences.text: Second, however, group work should not replace a substantial amount of lecture teaching.
Lectures remain an efficient way to deliver clear knowledge from an expert to many students.
Consider a difficult subject that students cannot grasp until a skilled teacher explains it clearly first.
Such cases show that group work alone can leave students confused and misinformed.
Group projects can also be uneven, with some students doing all the work and others little.
Too much group work could replace solid teaching with shallow and disorganised learning.
Collaboration, then, should add to lectures rather than largely replace them.
In conclusion, group assignments teach valuable collaboration that students truly need.
But they should not replace a substantial part of clear, expert lecturing.
The best courses combine group work with strong lectures, joining teamwork and clear instruction.
